front.title: HTTP/4: Mapping HTTP Semantics over the WIQC Decentralized Real-Time Torrent Transport Protocol

abstract.t: This document specifies HTTP/4, an application-layer mapping of HTTP semantics over a decentralized, peer-to-peer real-time streaming transport protocol named WIQC (Web-Integrated QUIC-derived Content-swarming). By design, the HTTP/4 protocol allows decentralized real-time streaming via a torrent protocol called not QUIC but WIQC. While HTTP/3 delegates stream multiplexing and congestion control to unicast client-server QUIC connections, HTTP/4 extends these capabilities to multipoint peer swarms. WIQC integrates encrypted UDP stream multiplexing with fine-grained cryptographic block verification using SHA-256 Merkle hash trees, live sliding-window chunk addressing, Unified Merkle Tree signatures for low-latency live streams, mutual peer authentication without centralized certificate authorities, and native UDP hole punching. This specification defines the wire framing, stream mapping, swarm discovery headers, real-time object prioritization, and security properties required to operate HTTP/4 natively across decentralized networks.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The architectural evolution of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol has progressively decoupled high-level application semantics from underlying transport bindings. While HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 rely primarily on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections, HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto the QUIC transport protocol to eliminate transport-layer head-of-line blocking and reduce handshake latency. However, HTTP/3 remains fundamentally bound to a centralized, unicast client-server topology. Real-time media delivery and large-scale content distribution over HTTP/3 still require centralized Content Delivery Network (CDN) relay infrastructures .
This document establishes the foundational mandate for the next generation of web transport:
The HTTP/4 protocol will allow decentralized real time streaming via torrent protocol called not QUIC but WIQC.

To fulfill this mandate, this specification defines WIQC (Web-Integrated QUIC-derived Content-swarming) as the underlying transport layer for HTTP/4. Rather than treating a resource origin as a single IP endpoint, HTTP/4 treats content representations and live media tracks as cryptographically verifiable swarms. Peers participating in an HTTP/4 exchange simultaneously act as consumers and relays, exchanging independent streams and unreliable datagrams across a decentralized mesh.
WIQC synthesizes four core protocol mechanisms into a unified transport layer:

list.t: Multiplexed Encrypted Framing: Derived from , providing connection migration, 0-RTT/1-RTT setup, and independent per-stream flow control.

Real-Time Swarm Integrity and Torrent Framing: Incorporating the bin-based chunk addressing, Live Discard Window, and Unified Merkle Tree live signature mechanisms of the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Peer Protocol (PPSPP) alongside the 16 KiB SHA-256 Merkle leaf verification of BitTorrent v2 .

Sub-Second Media Hierarchy: Adapting the Track, Group, Subgroup, and Object data model of Media over QUIC Transport so that each Subgroup maps to an independent unidirectional WIQC stream for immediate peer-to-peer forwarding and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling.

Decentralized Mutual Authentication and NAT Traversal: Utilizing self-signed X.509 certificates carrying the libp2p Public Key Extension over TLS 1.3 and native path-probing frames to establish direct peer-to-peer paths across Network Address Translators (NATs).

section.title: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words “MUST”, “MUST NOT”, “REQUIRED”, “SHALL”, “SHALL NOT”, “SHOULD”, “SHOULD NOT”, “RECOMMENDED”, “NOT RECOMMENDED”, “MAY”, and “OPTIONAL” in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the variable-length integer encoding and packet formatting conventions defined in Section 1.3 of .
The following terms are used throughout this specification:

list.t: WIQC Endpoint: A network node implementing the WIQC transport protocol capable of simultaneously initiating and accepting swarm streams as both an HTTP/4 client (subscriber/leecher) and an HTTP/4 peer server (publisher/seeder).

Swarm Identifier (Swarm ID): A cryptographic identifier uniquely representing an HTTP/4 resource or live stream. For static representations, the Swarm ID is the 32-byte SHA-256 Merkle root (pieces root) . For live streams, the Swarm ID is the public key fingerprint of the origin publisher .
Leaf Block: The smallest unit of cryptographic verification in WIQC, fixed at 16 KiB (16,384 bytes) in accordance with .

Munro Hash: An interior node root of a power-of-two subtree within a Unified Merkle Tree that is cryptographically signed by the live origin publisher via a SIGNED_INTEGRITY frame to authenticate dynamically generated live streaming chunks.
Subgroup Stream: A unidirectional WIQC stream carrying a sequence of media or data Objects that share a delivery priority and decoding dependency .

section.title: Relationship to QUIC and Peer-to-Peer Swarming
section.t: WIQC preserves the UDP packet framing, long and short headers, connection IDs, and per-stream reliability mechanisms of , but replaces the asymmetric client-server session model with a symmetric swarm channel model. A single HTTP/4 logical request can be satisfied concurrently by multiple WIQC connections to distinct peers participating in the same Swarm ID.

section.title: Swarm Handshake and Channel Multiplexing
section.t: During connection establishment or stream initialization, WIQC endpoints exchange swarm capabilities derived from and :

list.t: Swarm Metadata Negotiation: Endpoints negotiate the Swarm Identifier (Option Code 2), Content Integrity Protection Method (Option Code 3), Merkle Hash Tree Function (Option Code 4, fixed to SHA-256, code 0x02), Chunk Addressing Method (Option Code 6, defaulting to 64-bit bins, code 0x03), and Live Discard Window (Option Code 7) as defined in .

Anti-Amplification Rule: In accordance with and , an initiating peer’s first flight MUST NOT contain heavy payloads (such as DATA or SIGNED_INTEGRITY frames) prior to address validation via channel ID echoing or QUIC PATH_RESPONSE verification.

section.title: Cryptographic Integrity: Static and Live Torrent Modes
section.t: Because HTTP/4 peers receive byte ranges and real-time media frames from untrusted swarm participants, transport-level TLS 1.3 encryption only protects the hop-by-hop channel. End-to-end content integrity MUST be verified at the block or object level before data is passed to the HTTP/4 application or forwarded to other peers:

list.t: Static Content Mode (BEP 52 Merkle Mode): Content is divided into 16 KiB leaf blocks hashed with SHA-256 into a binary Merkle tree . Peers exchange standard peer wire protocol messages (IDs 21, 22, and 23 for hash request, hashes, and hash reject) to fetch missing uncle hashes required to verify a 16 KiB block immediately upon arrival. Corrupt blocks are discarded immediately, and the offending peer is isolated.

Decentralized Real-Time Streaming Mode (Unified Merkle Tree Mode): Since the total stream length is unknown ahead of time in live streaming, WIQC utilizes Content Integrity Protection Method 3 (Unified Merkle Tree) from . As the publisher generates new groups of real-time chunks, it computes the binary subtree root (the munro hash) covering the newly generated bin range, signs the munro hash using its private key, and distributes SIGNED_INTEGRITY and INTEGRITY frames across the swarm. Receiving peers verify each chunk against its munro branch before playback and immediately re-seed verified chunks to downstream peers.

section.title: Real-Time Streaming and Swarm Scheduling in HTTP/4
Media Data Model Mapping
section.t: To achieve sub-second real-time latency across a decentralized torrent swarm, HTTP/4 adopts the hierarchical data model of :

list.t: Track: Identified by a tuple of Track Namespace (bound to the HTTP/4 :authority and :path pseudo-headers) and Track Name (e.g., video bitrate variant, audio channel, or catalog track).
Group: A temporally bounded collection of objects starting at an independent synchronization point (such as an IDR keyframe), directly aligned with a WIQC Unified Merkle Tree munro subtree.

Subgroup: A subset of objects within a Group sharing a common priority and dependency chain. Each Subgroup MUST be mapped to exactly one unidirectional WIQC stream. If packet loss occurs on a lower-priority enhancement layer Subgroup, higher-priority base layer Subgroups proceed without head-of-line blocking.
Object: The smallest addressable media unit (e.g., a single encoded video frame or Low Overhead Container (LOC) payload).

section.title: Hybrid Earliest Deadline First (EDF) and Rarest-First Scheduling
section.t: Traditional torrent protocols rely purely on Rarest-First piece selection, which maximizes swarm diversity but ignores playback deadlines. Conversely, purely sequential fetching causes swarm starvation. WIQC endpoints implementing HTTP/4 real-time streaming MUST implement a dual-zone sliding window scheduler within the negotiated Live Discard Window , extending HTTP priority signaling :

list.t: Emergency Priority Zone (EDF Zone): For chunks whose playback deadline falls within a configurable threshold (e.g., < 150 ms), the peer requests missing Subgroups strictly in Earliest Deadline First (EDF) order from the lowest-RTT unchoked peers.

Swarm Health Zone (Rarest-First Zone): For chunks further ahead in the Live Discard Window, the peer uses remaining bandwidth to request the rarest chunks announced via HAVE frames, ensuring robust piece availability across the swarm.

section.title: HTTP/4 Stream Mapping
section.t: HTTP/4 preserves the stream categories of while introducing swarm-specific stream types:

texttable.c: Carries SETTINGS, GOAWAY, MAX_PUSH_ID, and swarm capabilities.
Server- or peer-initiated push of promised HTTP/4 representations.
Header table acknowledgments and stream cancellations per .
Carries a single real-time media Subgroup alongside its Merkle INTEGRITY proof.
Exchanges HAVE, REQUEST, CANCEL, CHOKE, UNCHOKE, and SIGNED_INTEGRITY frames.

section.title: HTTP/4 Frame Layout and Extensions
section.t: All HTTP/4 frames follow the variable-length integer framing layout of Section 7.1 of : Type (i), Length (i), and Frame Payload (..). In addition to DATA (0x00), HEADERS (0x01), CANCEL_PUSH (0x03), SETTINGS (0x04), PUSH_PROMISE (0x05), GOAWAY (0x07), and MAX_PUSH_ID (0x0d), HTTP/4 defines the following WIQC swarm frames:

texttable.c: Announces possession of verified 64-bit bin ranges .
Carries uncle hashes or Merkle branch proofs .
Carries publisher-signed munro root hashes for live streaming .
Peer Exchange (PEX_RESv4, PEX_RESv6, PEX_REQ) for trackerless discovery .

section.title: HTTP Header Fields for Swarm Integrity and Origin Authentication
section.t: When initiating a request or responding over HTTP/4, endpoints combine standard HTTP integrity and signature headers with WIQC swarm metadata:

list.t: Representation Digest (Repr-Digest and Content-Digest): In accordance with , static HTTP/4 responses MUST include a Repr-Digest header encoding the SHA-256 root hash, accompanied by a Swarm-Root dictionary field carrying the BEP 52 pieces root.

Origin Message Signatures (Signature-Input and Signature): Because HTTP/4 responses may be assembled from multiple untrusted peers, the origin server signs the response metadata (@status, content-type, repr-digest, and wiqc-swarm-id) using . Any peer in the swarm can forward the signed header block, and any receiving client can cryptographically verify that the metadata originated from the authoritative publisher.
Alternative Service and Discovery: Transition from unicast HTTP/3 or DNS resolution via SVCB/HTTPS records to HTTP/4 swarms is accomplished by advertising “h4” ALPN endpoints.

HTTP Datagrams and Capsule Protocol: Ultra-low-latency unreliable media objects MAY be transmitted via QUIC DATAGRAM frames associated with an HTTP/4 request stream, or encapsulated via the DATAGRAM Capsule (0x00) per when traversing HTTP intermediaries.

section.title: Decentralized Peer Authentication and NAT Traversal
Mutual TLS 1.3 with Self-Signed Peer Identity
section.t: In a decentralized torrent swarm, peers typically lack domain names and cannot obtain certificates from commercial PKIX Certificate Authorities (CAs). Therefore, WIQC mandates mutual authentication over TLS 1.3 using the libp2p TLS handshake mechanism :

list.t: Both dialing and listening WIQC endpoints MUST present a single self-signed X.509 certificate during the TLS 1.3 handshake (chains longer than one certificate MUST cause connection termination).
The certificate MUST include the libp2p Public Key Extension identified by Object Identifier (OID) 1.3.6.1.4.1.53594.1.1.

The extension contains an ASN.1-encoded SignedKey structure holding the peer’s public host key (e.g., Ed25519) and a cryptographic signature over the concatenation of the ASCII string “libp2p-tls-handshake:” and the DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo of the ephemeral certificate key.

For browser-based HTTP/4 endpoints operating over WebTransport, where the browser enforces CA checks or certificate pinning, endpoints MAY authenticate peers by embedding the certificate hash (certhash) in the peer advertisement and performing an in-band cryptographic binding handshake on the first stream.

section.title: Native WIQC NAT Traversal
section.t: To enable direct peer-to-peer streaming between home and mobile nodes behind NATs without relying on external ICE/STUN/TURN stacks, WIQC incorporates the native QUIC NAT traversal extension :

list.t: Well-connected relay or seed peers inform joining peers of their external UDP socket address using the OBSERVED_ADDRESS frame.

Peers advertise candidate addresses over existing swarm connections using ADD_ADDRESS (0x3d7e90..0x3d7e91) and REMOVE_ADDRESS (0x3d7e94) frames, and coordinate simultaneous UDP hole punching via PUNCH_ME_NOW (0x3d7e92..0x3d7e93) or grant-based PUNCH_REQUEST frames followed by standard PATH_CHALLENGE and PATH_RESPONSE validation .

section.title: Formal Syntax (ABNF)
section.t: The following Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) grammar defines the syntax of the WIQC-Swarm-Info HTTP header field and the h4 Alternative Service discovery token:

figure.artwork:
WIQC-Swarm-Info = "swarm-id=" byte-sequence ";" "mode=" ( "merkle-v2" / "unified-live" ) [ ";window=" 1*DIGIT ] [ ";chunk-addr=" ( "bin32" / "bin64" ) ]
byte-sequence = ":" *( BASE64CHAR ) ":" BASE64CHAR = ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "/" / "="
h4-alpn-id = %x68.34 ; "h4" in ASCII wiqc-alpn-id = %x77.69.71.63 ; "wiqc" in ASCII

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: This section analyzes the threat model of HTTP/4 over WIQC in accordance with .

section.title: Stream Pollution Attacks in Decentralized Swarms
section.t: In peer-to-peer live streaming, a malicious peer with high upload bandwidth can inject corrupted chunks (“pollution attack”) to degrade playback across the swarm. WIQC mitigates this by enforcing mandatory cryptographic verification before forwarding: every 16 KiB block in static mode is verified against the SHA-256 Merkle root , and every live chunk in Unified Merkle Tree mode is verified against a publisher-signed munro hash . Merkle-tree chaining keeps cryptographic verification bandwidth overhead around 5% (as evaluated under 128-bit MD5 and 1024-bit RSA reference parameters) while enabling deterministic identification and immediate banning of polluting peers.

section.title: Reflection and Amplification Attacks
section.t: Because WIQC operates over UDP, unverified source IP addresses pose a reflection amplification risk. Endpoints MUST enforce the anti-amplification limits of and MUST echo the peer’s randomly chosen Channel ID per Section 12.1 of before transmitting heavy payloads such as DATA or SIGNED_INTEGRITY messages.

section.title: Compression Side Channels and Replay Risks
section.t: When using QPACK in HTTP/4, endpoints MUST NOT compress sensitive authentication tokens alongside attacker-controlled data within the same dynamic table context (Section 10.6 of ). Furthermore, 0-RTT swarm requests MUST only be used for idempotent operations (such as subscribing to public live tracks) to prevent replay attacks.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

The Peer-to-Peer Streaming Peer Protocol (PPSPP) is a protocol for disseminating the same content to a group of interested parties in a streaming fashion. PPSPP supports streaming of both prerecorded (on- demand) and live audio/video content. It is based on the peer-to- peer paradigm, where clients consuming the content are put on equal footing with the servers initially providing the content, to create a system where everyone can potentially provide upload bandwidth. It has been designed to provide short time-till-playback for the end user and to prevent disruption of the streams by malicious peers. PPSPP has also been designed to be flexible and extensible. It can use different mechanisms to optimize peer uploading, prevent freeriding, and work with different peer discovery schemes (centralized trackers or Distributed Hash Tables). It supports multiple methods for content integrity protection and chunk addressing. Designed as a generic protocol that can run on top of various transport protocols, it currently runs on top of UDP using Low Extra Delay Background Transport (LEDBAT) for congestion control.

This document specifies "Alternative Services" for HTTP, which allow an origin's resources to be authoritatively available at a separate network location, possibly accessed with a different protocol configuration.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

abstract.t: This document defines the core of the QUIC transport protocol. QUIC provides applications with flow-controlled streams for structured communication, low-latency connection establishment, and network path migration. QUIC includes security measures that ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability in a range of deployment circumstances. Accompanying documents describe the integration of TLS for key negotiation, loss detection, and an exemplary congestion control algorithm.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The QUIC transport protocol has several features that are desirable in a transport for HTTP, such as stream multiplexing, per-stream flow control, and low-latency connection establishment. This document describes a mapping of HTTP semantics over QUIC. This document also identifies HTTP/2 features that are subsumed by QUIC and describes how HTTP/2 extensions can be ported to HTTP/3.

This specification defines QPACK: a compression format for efficiently representing HTTP fields that is to be used in HTTP/3. This is a variation of HPACK compression that seeks to reduce head-of-line blocking.

This document describes a scheme that allows an HTTP client to communicate its preferences for how the upstream server prioritizes responses to its requests, and also allows a server to hint to a downstream intermediary how its responses should be prioritized when they are forwarded. This document defines the Priority header field for communicating the initial priority in an HTTP version-independent manner, as well as HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frames for reprioritizing responses. These share a common format structure that is designed to provide future extensibility.

front.title: An Unreliable Datagram Extension to QUIC

abstract.t: This document defines an extension to the QUIC transport protocol to add support for sending and receiving unreliable datagrams over a QUIC connection.

front.title: HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes HTTP Datagrams, a convention for conveying multiplexed, potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection.

In HTTP/3, HTTP Datagrams can be sent unreliably using the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. When the QUIC DATAGRAM frame is unavailable or undesirable, HTTP Datagrams can be sent using the Capsule Protocol, which is a more general convention for conveying data in HTTP connections.
HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol are intended for use by HTTP extensions, not applications.

This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

front.title: Service Binding and Parameter Specification via the DNS (SVCB and HTTPS Resource Records)

abstract.t: This document specifies the "SVCB" ("Service Binding") and "HTTPS" DNS resource record (RR) types to facilitate the lookup of information needed to make connections to network services, such as for HTTP origins. SVCB records allow a service to be provided from multiple alternative endpoints, each with associated parameters (such as transport protocol configuration), and are extensible to support future uses (such as keys for encrypting the TLS ClientHello). They also enable aliasing of apex domains, which is not possible with CNAME. The HTTPS RR is a variation of SVCB for use with HTTP (see RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics"). By providing more information to the client before it attempts to establish a connection, these records offer potential benefits to both performance and privacy.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

front.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.

This document obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3. This document obsoletes RFC 5246 (specifying TLS 1.2) and RFCs 5077, 6961, 7627, and 8422, all of which pertain to TLS 1.2 or earlier, and updates RFCs 5705 and 6066. This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations

abstract.t: All RFCs are required to have a Security Considerations section. Historically, such sections have been relatively weak. This document provides guidelines to RFC authors on how to write a good Security Considerations section. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

This document defines Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT), a publish/ subscribe protocol that runs over QUIC and WebTransport. MOQT leverages the features of these transports, such as streams, datagrams, priorities, and partial reliability. MOQT operates both point-to-point and through intermediate relays, enabling scalable low-latency delivery. Despite its name, MOQT is media agnostic and can be used for a wide range of use cases.

This document specifies a QUIC extension for traversing Network Address Translators (NATs). Endpoints use an existing proxied QUIC connection to coordinate path validation attempts that create the NAT bindings needed for a direct path and test its connectivity. Application data can be exchanged over the proxied path while NAT traversal is in progress. Once a suitable direct path has been validated, the connection can migrate to it.
